Double B Studio
@Clems822
I disagree with this statement: Here I need to remind myslef that most of all, this is designer's challenge, so the art should not play the prime in rating. I understand that some designer are more interested to create unique mechanics and are not interested or skilled in graphics, but I'm not appealed by games without good graphic design. My favourite games have incredible mechanics and incredible graphic design. If it is lacking in of the 2, it's difficult for me to fully love it.
It's my personal preset and it is totally okay if you have your preferences skewed towards certain direction more than to another. In this contest (and contests alike) I try to look at the designs with more widespread optics, trying to find something worthy alongside visuals and general fun playing the game as I was in the same camp of people who just sketched quick design and pushed it under the noses of friends to playtest it. Then, after they started to revoke my hand-drawn designs (cardstock+markers style!) in comparison to all the produced games we were playing, I pushed myself to focus on the visuals as well. I am still nowhere near to professional design with my games, but I may say I try my best to make them as visually... acceptable as the prototypes need to be.

To be fair, sometimes it is really hard to find the good in the games where designers ignore at least basic layout guidelines, formatting the rules as flow of the mind, or endless numbered lists. Sure, some people think structurally and lists like these help them to grasp the rules easier, but market shows us that rules has to be written in a human form and with human touch as well. And the same is applied to visuals of the components as well. It's hard to submerge into some deep theme if game components look like they hit their second iteration after initial idea.

To sum that up: if this contest was presented as "ready to production" contest, I would be much more critical to the visuals of the games. With current state though I am fine with my AMIGO rating system, where aesthetics make only fifth of the overall score.

For games using standard decks I use slightly altered SCORE system, where the visuals rating is omitted completely.

I have to say, I was not expecting to open BGG today and see this notification waiting for me. It’s honestly mind-blowing to me that my little shrinko project won first place in one of my favorite BGG design contests. I want to extend a huge thank you to everyone at Side Room Games for hosting the contest and choosing The Cubes of Europe for the jury prize, and an equally huge thanks to the many supportive and helpful playtesters who gave feedback on the game throughout the contest.

I also want to thank everyone who participated in the contest as well - there were a ton of great games this year, and I’m sure it was a tough decision for the judges to choose between the more than 30 games that entered. This contest wouldn’t be what it is without the huge group of designers who support and help each other even when competing; that’s one of the things I love about BGG. 

I’m not really sure how to end this post, so I’ll just say thank you again to everyone at Side Room Games for hosting this great contest, and I’m looking forward to seeing where The Cubes of Europe could go in the future.
